$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((y-4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)) \\  & =\frac{y-4}{x-2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((y-4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\nabla f(x,y) = \dfrac {y-4}{x-2} \, \mathbf i + \ln(x-2) \, \mathbf j.
$$

Now, we solve $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf 0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\dfrac {y-4}{x-2} \, \mathbf i + \ln(x-2) \, \mathbf j = 0 \  \mathbf i + 0\ \mathbf j
$$

By equating the coefficients of $\mathbf{i}$ on both sides of the equation (and similarly with $\mathbf{j}$), we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{y-4}{x-2}=0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $y-4=0,$ which means $y=4.$  From the second equation, we obtain $\ln(x-2)=0,$ which means that $x=3.$

Therefore, $\nabla f(x,y) =\mathbf  0$ at the point $(3,4).$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124447 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-5961ee6e-358e-5baa-837e-dbd941cc54b6"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-51a75799-7672-5c71-a422-88f2c2c1de7a" :question/id #uuid "51a75799-7672-5c71-a422-88f2c2c1de7a" :question/math-academy-id "q-127652" :question/problem "Evaluate $∇f(x,y)$ at $(e,1)$ if $f(x,y)={x}^{y}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the partial derivatives:

$h(x,y,z)=xy{e}^{x}+{z}^{2}{e}^{z}.$ Find the points $(x,y,z)$ where $∇h(x,y,z)=0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy{e}^{x}+{z}^{2}{e}^{z}) \\  & =xy{e}^{x}+y{e}^{x}+0 \\  & =y(x+1){e}^{x} \\ {h}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy{e}^{x}+{z}^{2}{e}^{z}) \\  & =x{e}^{x}+0 \\  & =x{e}^{x} \\ {h}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy{e}^{x}+{z}^{2}{e}^{z}) \\  & =0+2z{e}^{z}+{z}^{2}{e}^{z} \\  & =z(2+z){e}^{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇h(x,y,z)=y(x+1){e}^{x}\,i+x{e}^{x}\,j+z(2+z){e}^{z}\,k.$

Now, we solve $∇f(x,y,z)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x+1){e}^{x}\,i+x{e}^{x}\,j+z(2+z){e}^{z}\,k & =0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j+0\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$, $j$, and $k$, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y(x+1){e}^{x}=0 \\ x{e}^{x}=0 \\ z(2+z){e}^{z}=0\end{aligned}
$$

The second equation gives $x=0.$ Substituting these into the first equation, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0+1){e}^{0} & =0 \\ y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, from the third equation, we get  $z=0$ or $z=-2.$

Therefore, $∇h(x,y,z)=0$ at two points: $(0,0,0)$ and $(0,0,-2).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e83f4999-419d-51c4-a803-c6789f4e1b52"] :question/math-academy-id "q-128513" :question/problem "Given $h(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+4yz-2{z}^{2}-2{y}^{2}x.$ Find the points $(x,y,z)$ where $∇h(x,y,z)=0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+4yz-2{z}^{2}-2{y}^{2}x) \\  & =2x-2{y}^{2} \\ {h}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+4yz-2{z}^{2}-2{y}^{2}x) \\  & =4z-4yx \\ {h}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+4yz-2{z}^{2}-2{y}^{2}x) \\  & =4y-4z\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇h(x,y,z)=2(x-{y}^{2})\,i+4(z-yx)\,j+4(y-z)\,k.$

Now, we solve $∇f(x,y,z)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(x-{y}^{2})\,i+4(z-yx)\,j+4(y-z)\,k & =0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j+0\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$, $j$, and $k$, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x-{y}^{2}=0, \\ z-yx=0, \\ y-z=0\end{aligned}
$$

The first equation gives $x={y}^{2}.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain $z={y}^{3}.$ Substituting $z={y}^{3}$ into the third equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}^{3} & =0 \\ y(1-{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ y & =0,\,\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y=-1,$ we get $x=(-1)^{2}=1$ and $z=(-1)^{3}=-1.$

- For $y=0,$ we obtain $x={0}^{2}=0$ and $z={0}^{3}=0.$

- For $y=1,$ gives $x={1}^{2}=1$ and $z={1}^{3}=1.$

Finally, $∇h(x,y,z)=0$ at three points: $(1,-1,-1),$ $(0,0,0)$ and $(1,1,1).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields :question/math-academy-id "q-71515" :question/problem "What is the gradient of the product $f(x,y)h(x,y)$ if $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}$ and $h(x,y)=y{e}^{x}?$" :question/worked-solution "The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fh]=f\,∇\,h+h\,∇\,f\,\,
$$

Now, we calculate the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y})={e}^{y} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y})=x{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Find the points $(x,y,z)$ where $∇h(x,y,z)=0.$"] ["question-d13fce5d-8bd4-547a-afec-720ff5befaa7" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$

Hence, $∇h(x,y,z)=y(x+1){e}^{x}\,i+x{e}^{x}\,j+z(2+z){e}^{z}\,k.$

$$

$$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y(x+1){e}^{x}=0 \\ x{e}^{x}=0 \\ z(2+z){e}^{z}=0\end{aligned}
$$

The second equation gives $x=0.$ Substituting these into the first equation, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0+1){e}^{0} & =0 \\ y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$h(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fh]=f\,∇\,h+h\,∇\,f\,\,
$$

Now, we calculate the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y})={e}^{y} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y})=x{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\text{ }j={e}^{y}\text{ }i+x{e}^{y}\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of $h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y{e}^{x})=y{e}^{x} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{x})={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y) & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\text{ }j=y{e}^{x}\text{ }i+{e}^{x}\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the product rule, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)h(x,y)] & =x{e}^{y}(y{e}^{x}\text{ }i+{e}^{x}\text{ }j)+y{e}^{x}({e}^{y}\text{ }i+x{e}^{y}\text{ }j) \\  & =xy{e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+x{e}^{x+y}\text{ }j+y{e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+xy{e}^{x+y}\text{ }j \\  & =(x+1)y{e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+x(1+y){e}^{x+y}\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-5961ee6e-358e-5baa-837e-dbd941cc54b6" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-90c23b7b-1640-5aaa-b8b3-64340afb293e" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$
\nabla f(x,y) = \dfrac {y-4}{x-2} \, \mathbf i + \ln(x-2) \, \mathbf j.
$$

$$
\dfrac {y-4}{x-2} \, \mathbf i + \ln(x-2) \, \mathbf j = 0 \  \mathbf i + 0\ \mathbf j
$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{y-4}{x-2}=0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $y-4=0,$ which means $y=4.$  From the second equation, we obtain $\ln(x-2)=0,$ which means that $x=3.$
